topic: The frequency illusion ('Baader-Meinhof'): why you suddenly see it everywhere
title: Why You Suddenly See It Everywhere
voiceover: Ever learn a new word, then see it everywhere? Linguist Arnold Zwicky called this the frequency illusion. It's also called the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon, a name that came from a 1994 letter to a newspaper column. Both names come from informal sources, not experiments. A related, well-tested finding is that attention is limited. In Simons and Chabris's 1999 invisible-gorilla study, viewers counted basketball passes. Many failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene. That shows we can miss things we aren't paying attention to. One idea is that once something captures your attention, you start noticing what you previously missed. So if something suddenly seems to be everywhere, ask whether it increased, or whether you simply started noticing. Tomorrow: do decisions really wear your brain out?

description: Ever learn a new word and then see it everywhere? Linguist Arnold Zwicky called it the frequency illusion, and a famous attention study shows we miss much of what we're not focused on. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Zwicky, A. M. (2005). Just between Dr. Language and I (Language Log post introducing 'frequency illusion'). Language Log (blog). Source: Simons, D. J., & Chabris, C. F. (1999). Gorillas in our midst: Sustained inattentional blindness for dynamic events. Perception, 28(9), 1059-1074.
accuracy_note: INFORMAL TERM. 'Frequency illusion' and 'Baader-Meinhof phenomenon' come from a linguist's blog and a newspaper letter, not from lab experiments. The explanation (attention and noticing) is a widely offered idea, not directly tested in the cited studies; Simons & Chabris demonstrates limits of attention, not the frequency illusion itself. The video hedges with 'one idea'.
